newsitem.title: JAPAN: Social Democrats set new hurdle for Hashimoto.
newsitem.headline: Social Democrats set new hurdle for Hashimoto.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's bid to form a new coalition met a further hurdle on Thursday when the Social Democrats, partners in his previous government, insisted on policy agreements before deciding whether to join.
"The fundamental issue is to seek an agreement over policy," Social Democrat leader Takako Doi said in a statement after a meeting of her party's executive board.
"It is wrong to argue about joining either the opposition or ruling camp without an agreement on policy," she said.
Doi confirmed her party's decision to enter into policy negotiations with Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which could start sometime next week, party officials said.
In last Sunday's general election, Hashimoto's party won 239 seats in the powerful Lower House, 12 short of a majority.
Hashimoto needs the 15 Lower House seats and 32 Upper House seats held by the Social Democrats to command a working majority in both houses of parliament.
Hashimoto has also been trying to lure the tiny Sakigake party and the fledgling Democratic Party but has not started formal negotiations with any party.
The two lawmakers in Sakigake have said they would most likely join the coalition, but the Democrats have been cool to the idea.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama has said the government aims to reconvene parliament on November 7 for a special session to elect the new prime minister.
Hashimoto's government stays on as caretaker until a new prime minister is formally elected by parliament.
Social Democrat lawmakers in the Upper House are keen to join forces with the LDP but Doi said she was reluctant to do so because of her party's sagging fortunes.
In the opposition camp, the main group Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) is licking its wounds after a failed move to break up the party following its poor election showing.
Shinshinto was aiming for a Lower House majority but ended up with just 156 seats in the 500-member Lower House, four fewer than in the previous parliament.
Maverick party leader Ichiro Ozawa came under pressure to step down this week, mainly because of his forceful manner in running party affairs.
On Tuesday party member and ex-premier Morihiro Hosokawa told a party meeting that Shinshinto should aim for a "negotiated divorce", meaning an amicable split.
The rebellion was ended after Shinshinto support groups, including a huge Buddhist group and trade unions, told the two to stop the infighting, Shinshinto lawmakers said.
"I must apologise for the confusion I brought on," party officials quoted Hosokawa as telling a party meeting on Thursday.
